Round two: leave, the top section, and the tables

Samples only. Nothing has been changed in the app for this round. Every board, mission card, employee card, leave zone and table below is the app's own markup rendered with its own styles.css, loaded with data that matches your screenshots: 106 people, 72 assigned (65 day, 7 night), 22 on leave including 19 on exchange days, 12 on-call free, and your seven areas. Use the switches above each mock to compare.

What I found in your screenshots

Leave area today

  1. Nothing lines up. The groups sit on one row at different widths with different gaps, so no edge or column carries from one group to the next.
  2. Dashed slots read as missing cards. Every group with people ends in an empty dashed box. There are three of them, and each looks like a card that failed to load.
  3. The empty type floats. "Business Leave 0" sits alone in the middle of the row, between two groups that have people.
  4. Two layouts in one band. The 19-person Exchange Working Day starts a second row with a different indent from the "Leave" label, so the band reads as a row plus a block.
  5. Labels are inconsistent. Each label mixes a bold name, small Thai text and a count pill, and the pill sits at a different distance from the name every time.
  6. Exchange days are not leave. They sit under the word "Leave" and, with 19 people, take most of the height.

Top section and panel today

  1. Four bands before any content. Banner, tabs, toolbar, then stats and area chips: the leave area starts 237 px down the screen.
  2. Eleven controls of the same weight. New Mission, New Employee, Holiday, four filters, Hide, Sort, Undo and Reset all look alike, and Names and Export sit on the row below.
  3. Filters look like actions. Engineer, Host, Customer and Shift are four more buttons that open nothing but a filter list.
  4. The most-used tab is not distinct. The boards share a row with Overview, Org chart and the other modules, with only a thin rule between them.
  5. The panel starts beside the banner. The people panel runs from the very top of the screen, so the search box sits level with the logo and the banner is cut short.
  6. A three-way dropdown for a two-way choice. Names offers Thai, English and Thai + English.

Manpower table today

Host table today

  1. Empty columns are always drawn. Mobile number, Start date and Years of service show "—" in every row of this data. That is 3 of 11 columns of nothing.
  2. The same signal 106 times. Every active person carries a green switch and the word "Active". Only the rare inactive row needs to stand out.
  3. Area pills outshout the names. Filled magenta, blue and yellow pills are the loudest thing in each row.
  4. Headers shout and utilization draws empty bars. The headers are all caps with wide tracking, and the 30-day bar track draws at full length even at 0 percent.
  5. Host: repeated placeholders. "+ Add note" and "No one deployed yet" repeat on all 16 rows. The Note column is the widest and mostly empty.
  6. Host: a loud banner and uneven rows. Duplicate names raise a full-width amber bar above the table, and a wrapped note makes some rows taller than others.
  7. Two bands of controls. Search, the names dropdown and six equal filter buttons sit in one band, and the stat chips with Bulk edit and Export in the next.

Leave options

All four keep the employee cards exactly as they are. The dashed "ghost" slots are gone: a lane is a drop target as a whole, and it outlines when you drag over it. The Exchange Working Day (19 people) is what makes this hard, so each option handles it differently.

Rows Original rows, for reference

  • One full-width row per type, label cell on the left, cards wrapping to the right.
  • Always aligned and every card visible, but it is the tallest option.

A Five lanes

  • Five lanes in one band: four narrow ones plus a wide Exchange lane. Same header style on every lane, no ghost slots.
  • Always aligned and every lane is a visible drop target.
  • A lane holds about two rows and scrolls inside, so most of the 19 exchange people are out of sight until you scroll the lane.

B Tabs with counts

  • One lane open at a time, chosen from tabs that show every count. It opens on the busiest type.
  • Calmest and shortest on a quiet day, and every card in the open lane is visible.
  • Only one lane is visible, so a drag needs the tabs to take drops too (hover to open).

C Four lanes, exchange days underneath

  • The four real leave types sit in four equal, aligned lanes. Exchange Working Day gets its own full-width lane underneath because it is a different thing.
  • All five are visible drop targets. The exchange lane shows one row and a "Show all 19" button that remembers its state.

My recommendation: C. It is the only option that explains why the layout looks the way it does: four leave types in one aligned grid, and the odd one out (exchange days) on its own full-width line. With Exchange collapsed it saves about 299 px against the original rows (from 597 px to 298 px), keeps every drop target on screen, and does not hide the other lanes. A is the shortest at 233 px but most of the 19 exchange people sit inside a scrolling lane. B is the same height as C on this day, and shows only one lane at a time.

Top section options

In every option the banner holds the module tabs, Sign out moves into the avatar menu, and the people panel tucks under the banner. Filters and Sort share one "Filter & sort" popover, and Holiday and Reset board move into "⋯". Names is a two-way Thai | English toggle.

1 Banner tabs

  • Modules in the navy banner. A white bar below holds the board switcher, status and all actions. Then the stats strip with area chips.
  • Most familiar. The boards stay prominent as a switcher.

2 Navy control deck

  • Modules in row one, boards and every action in a second navy row. Only the stats strip is white.
  • Fewest bands of different colour: one dark block, one light strip. Buttons on navy need their own styling.

3 Compact

  • The board becomes a dropdown in the banner. One white bar for actions, and the stats shrink to one inline line with the area chips.
  • Shortest by far. Stats and boards are less prominent.

My recommendation: 1. The three options give back a similar amount of height (about 49, 57 and 59 px), so choose on structure. Option 1 keeps the boards visible as a switcher, reads as two clear zones (navigate in the banner, act in the white bar) and needs the least new styling. Option 2 has the strongest identity if you like dark controls. Option 3 gives the most room back but turns the boards into a dropdown and shrinks the stats. In all three the people panel now runs the full height below the banner, with the toolbar and stats to its left.

Table options: Manpower and Host

These are the real tables with the real rows. In the Quiet and Grouped options the markup is the same table with new styling. The Directory option changes the markup. The toolbar above the table is the same in all three: one search box, one Filters button (with a count when something is set), the Thai | English toggle, and the counts and actions on the right.

Tab
Table

A Quiet table

  • Sentence-case headers, 46 px rows, hairlines only.
  • Columns with no data are hidden and "—" is blank, so the three empty Manpower columns disappear.
  • Area is a colour key beside the name instead of a filled pill. The Active switch is smaller, navy and wordless; only Archived or Inactive show a label.
  • Host: "+ Add note" appears on row hover, "No one deployed yet" is simply left blank, and the duplicates notice becomes a slim bar.

B People directory

  • Two-line first column: an avatar, the name, and "TRIGO ID · position" underneath. Fewer, clearer columns and 58 px rows.
  • Contract is only marked when it is On-call. Host: name with location underneath, so the Location column goes away.
  • Friendliest to read. It changes the markup, so it is the most work and touches the table tests.

C Dense, grouped by area

  • 36 px rows under sticky group headers per service area, with the head count. The Service area column is dropped because the group is the area.
  • Best for scanning 106 people by site. It would be a "Group by" choice, because grouping only makes sense when sorting by area.
My recommendation: A for both tables, with C as a "Group by area" option. A removes the noise without changing the structure, so it is quick and low risk, and it keeps sorting, bulk edit and the existing tests working. B is the most pleasant to read but is a rebuild. All three would use the same toolbar.
